prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated together, bringing optical timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B037, Katori and Ye. After reading the full first-round exchange the case looks stronger to me, not weaker, because the objections raised were about wording and overlap and none was about the physics. The new idea is simple to state. A standing wave of light normally shifts the atomic transition it holds, which ruins a clock. At the magic wavelength the shift of the two clock levels is the same, so it cancels, and thousands of neutral atoms can be held still and interrogated together. That is what gives the stability that single ions cannot reach, and it later led Ye's group into a regime in which interactions among the atoms matter, which no ion clock addresses. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by several laboratories and compared across continents, which is the kind of robustness I look for. It also says something about nature: clocks now resolve the gravitational redshift over a millimetre and bound drifts of fundamental constants. As Kroll notes, the blackbody-shift and magic-wavelength calculations are what make a 10^-18 uncertainty budget credible, so this is an example of theory and experiment closing on each other. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 1997, 2005 and 2012 prizes remains the real risk, and I do not think it can be argued away by assertion. My answer to the chair's second question is this: the 2005 prize gave the comb that links optical and microwave frequencies, and the 2012 prize gave control of single quantum systems, ion clocks included. Neither contains the lattice idea that the shift can be cancelled for a large ensemble, so the citation should say magic wavelength and many-atom interrogation, not optical clocks in general and not the redefinition of the second. The second weakness is credit. Writing from memory, not from the primary papers, I recall that Katori and collaborators proposed magic-wavelength trapping around 2001 to 2003 and demonstrated the strontium lattice clock in 2005, that Ye's group and the Paris group (Lemonde, Le Targat) followed in 2006 with independent measurements, and that Ye's group then took it to the 10^-16 and later 10^-18 level, with the many-body work after that. I could not settle precisely who was first at each step, and I do not think two names is wholly clean: Lemonde and the Paris group and the Boulder and NIST contributors have a real claim. I do not think that justifies a third name, since a padded citation would be weaker, but the committee should say so openly. This is also the field closest to my own, so I discount my own enthusiasm.

responses.point: Kroll argues that atomic theory is more central than I suggested, since the blackbody-shift and magic-wavelength calculations are what make the 10^-18 uncertainty budget credible, and that the committee should read the case as theory and experiment together.
responses.response: I accept the correction. I wrote my first-round case as an experimental story, and he is right that the magic-wavelength condition and the blackbody and lattice-light-shift corrections come from atomic structure calculations that people in my own subfield do. I would still not add a theorist as a third name. The calculations are a supporting method, many groups share them, and the shortlist offers no theory name that the other seven members agree on. That is better handled in the discussion of the work than in the credit. I do agree with him that the citation should name the magic wavelength explicitly, because that is where the theory enters, and I agree that we should leave the redefinition of the second out of the citation.

responses.point: Pearce asks that atomic-physics colleagues confirm formally that the lattice clock differs from the 2012 ion-control prize, wants the priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium clock and the JILA accuracy work checked, and says the redefinition of the second argues for timeliness, not merit.
responses.response: I will answer both parts as far as I can without the papers in front of me. On what is new, I stand by the statement above: the 2012 prize was for preparing and reading out single quantum systems, and the lattice clock gets its stability from interrogating many atoms at once with the lattice shift cancelled. On priority, my recollection is a proposal with a first demonstration from Katori's group, independent confirmation in 2006, and Ye's group driving accuracy and coherence and many-body physics, so the roles are separable. But it is from memory, and I recommend that the final ballots be taken with an expert report or the primary papers behind them, as he asks. I agree that the redefinition belongs to timeliness and not to merit, and my citation now omits it.

responses.point: Olsson asks the atomic-physics members to say whether the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct discovery or an evolutionary step, because that decides whether B037 is an original experiment or a better one, and she has moved to B042 as her preferred choice.
responses.response: I think it is a distinct step, for a reason that does not depend on the figures of merit. Before the magic wavelength, trapping neutral atoms in light and measuring an optical transition were incompatible, because the trap shifted the line. The magic wavelength removed that obstacle in principle and in practice, and that is a new capability, not just a smaller uncertainty. It also gave access to the ensemble regime in which collisions and interactions between atoms matter. I would still say honestly that it is an invention more than a discovery of a new phenomenon, and if the committee holds that against it, the question for B042 is the converse: whether a prediction and an observation in HgTe can stand without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. I cannot judge that, and I defer to her and the other condensed-matter members, but I remain with B037 for now.

responses.point: Danielsson says his own first choice B006 has an attribution problem, since the three names are founding spokespersons, and that B037 has crisper credit and broader support; B037 is his first alternative.
responses.response: I am glad that he names B037 as his fallback, and I respect how openly he states the credit difficulty. He asks how the committee should define the three names. I cannot supply a rationale from outside particle physics, and I think the chair's question about who the decisive contributors were at the time of discovery is better answered by him and Pearce than by me. I will say that the discovery was a measurement by two collaborations of a particle whose existence the 2013 prize had already honoured theoretically, and a prize to three founders of detectors would honour construction and leadership more than the discovery. If a committee majority concludes that it can defend that wording, I would not block it, but I would rank it behind B037 and B042 today.

uncertainties: Priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock, and the later accuracy and many-body work: I am recalling it from memory and have not checked the primary papers, and the committee should see an expert check before it votes.
Whether the committee will judge the lattice clock to be a distinct invention beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or an evolutionary refinement of them.
Whether two names are fair to the Paris, Boulder and NIST contributors and to the ion-clock community, or whether the citation should say openly that others share the credit.

Whether B042 can be given a defensible three-name credit without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which is the one point that could move me to rank it alongside B037, though I defer to the condensed-matter members.
statement.conflict_note: No documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, and none of my connections involves a credited name on any shortlisted entry. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and Keller attosecond groups, and I belong to the same broad atomic, molecular and optical community as the clock groups, so my familiarity with the field may inflate my judgement and I would accept an expert check. Unchanged from round 1; I do not request recusal.
